blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpret diagnostic/laboratory results and recognize risk-reduction implications
stem: A 28-year-old client without known ASCVD has an LDL-C of 165 mg/dL. Which interpretation should the nurse recognize as most consistent with the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline?

options.A: Use PREVENT-ASCVD now to calculate 10-year risk and let that score determine whether lipid-lowering therapy should be discussed.
options.B: Continue lifestyle optimization and defer a medication discussion until age 30, when PREVENT-ASCVD risk calculation becomes applicable.
options.C: Use the restored LDL-C treatment goals alone to determine therapy because the 2026 guideline replaces individualized risk assessment with a single LDL-C goal.
options.D: Support lifestyle optimization and an earlier clinician-patient discussion about possible lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy because LDL-C is at least 160 mg/dL in young adulthood.

rationale: The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline emphasizes earlier prevention. Its Top Things to Know states that in young adulthood, LDL-C at least 160 mg/dL supports early consideration of pharmacotherapy while lifestyle optimization remains foundational. Therefore D is correct. A is incorrect because PREVENT-ASCVD is specified for adults aged 30 to 79 years, so it should not be applied to this 28-year-old as the basis for the decision. B is incorrect because the guideline specifically supports earlier consideration of pharmacotherapy in young adulthood at this LDL-C threshold rather than deferring the discussion until age 30. C is incorrect because although LDL-C treatment goals have returned, the guideline also directs individualized risk assessment and clinician-patient discussion rather than replacing them with one LDL-C value alone.
educational_objective: For a young adult with LDL-C at least 160 mg/dL, recognize that the 2026 ACC/AHA guideline supports lifestyle optimization plus early individualized discussion of lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy; PREVENT-ASCVD risk estimation is specified for adults aged 30 to 79 years.
source_organization: American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC)
source_document_title: 2026 Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia — Top Things to Know
source_locator: Top Things to Know #1: lifestyle optimization beginning in youth and early consideration of pharmacotherapy in young adulthood for LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL or strong family history of premature ASCVD; #2: PREVENT equations for primary-prevention risk assessment in adults aged 30–79 years with personalized risk discussion; #4: LDL-C/non-HDL-C treatment goals are used to guide therapy but do not replace individualized risk assessment.
source_claim_supported: A 28-year-old with LDL-C 165 mg/dL meets the guideline's young-adulthood LDL-C threshold for early consideration of pharmacotherapy alongside lifestyle optimization; PREVENT-ASCVD is specified for ages 30–79 and treatment remains individualized.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p.13/PDF p.17: monitor diagnostic test results and respond as appropriate; recognize trends/changes and take risk-reduction action. Distribution of Content, printed p.5/PDF p.9: Reduction of Risk Potential 9–15%.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the stem and all four options to remove absolute-word cueing, eliminate a generic educational objective, keep each alternative within the same guideline construct, and make the correct response explicitly nurse-scope recognition rather than independent prescribing.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Primary prevention dyslipidemia — young-adult LDL-C interpretation
audit_findings.stem: PASS — age, ASCVD status, and LDL-C are sufficient to apply the cited 2026 guideline statement without hidden assumptions.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — plausible because PREVENT is central to the 2026 guideline, but the guideline specifies PREVENT for ages 30–79, not age 28.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — plausible age-threshold confusion, but contradicted by the explicit recommendation for early pharmacotherapy consideration in young adulthood with LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — LDL-C goals did return in 2026, but the guideline still uses individualized risk assessment and clinician-patient discussion; goals are not a single stand-alone decision rule.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS — directly matches Top Things to Know #1 and preserves individualized clinician-patient discussion.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — D uniquely combines the correct young-adult LDL-C threshold with the guideline's early-prevention approach; A and B misuse age-based risk assessment, and C misstates the role of goals.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — no alternative is consistent with both the age-specific pharmacotherapy statement and the guideline's individualized risk framework.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — no distractor-only absolute term or obvious mechanism error remains; all options are guideline-management interpretations of comparable specificity.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — interpreting a laboratory result and recognizing its risk-reduction implications fits Reduction of Risk Potential; the item remains at application-level recognition rather than specialty prescribing.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether age 28 should force deferral until PREVENT eligibility and whether restored LDL-C goals create a second answer. The 2026 AHA/ACC source explicitly supports early consideration of pharmacotherapy in young adults with LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL and separately limits PREVENT use to ages 30–79 while retaining personalized risk discussion. D remains uniquely best.
